hints.title: Break a long integral into unit intervals
hints.body: For a positive integer r, split ∫0rf(x)dx at the integer boundaries. Each piece then has exactly the form described in the question.
hints.recap: Adjacent definite integrals add when their endpoints meet.
hints.pitfall: The index in the given rule is the lower endpoint of a unit interval.
hints.pause: Write the pieces for the first few cumulative integrals.

recall.reminder: Adjacent definite integrals add when their endpoints meet.

hints.title: Keep a running total
hints.body: The values of successive unit-interval integrals form an arithmetic progression. To form each term of the outer sum, first add all the unit pieces from zero up to its upper limit.
hints.recap: A sum of cumulative totals is different from one final cumulative total.
hints.pitfall: Do not replace the sum of eight integrals by only the integral with the largest upper limit.
hints.pause: Compute each cumulative total, using an arithmetic-series formula or a running total, and then add the eight results.

recall.reminder: A sum of cumulative totals is different from one final cumulative total.

solution:
1. Add adjacent unit intervals. For each positive integer r, ∫0rf(x)dx=∑n=0r−1∫nn+1f(x)dx=1+2+⋯+r=r(r+1)2.

2. Evaluate the outer sum. For r=1,2,…,8, the cumulative integrals are 1,3,6,10,15,21,28,36. Adding them gives 120.

Answer C. As a check, the unit interval with integral 1 appears eight times, the one with integral 2 appears seven times, and so on; 8·1+7·2+6·3+5·4+4·5+3·6+2·7+1·8=120.
knowledgePattern: Build cumulative integrals from unit intervals and sum their totals
